statement: Three lily pads are called A, B and C. A frog on A makes 3 jumps, each time to one of the other two pads. In how many ways can it finish on B?

choices.misconception: I counted only the trips whose first jump goes to B.
I thought exactly half of all the trips must end on B.
I counted every trip that does not end back on A, including the ones ending on C.
I counted every possible trip of 3 jumps, wherever it ends.

hints: Draw a tree starting at A, with two branches for each jump.
Each jump gives two branches, so 3 jumps make a small tree. Write the pad reached at each step and count only the branches that finish on B.
The trips that finish on B are A, B, A, B and A, B, C, B and A, C, A, B. That is 3 ways.

solutions.reliable: Tree from A. Jump 1 goes to B or C. From B the frog can go to A or C, and from C to A or B. Jump 3 can land on B only if jump 2 did not. The trips are A, B, A, B and A, B, C, B and A, C, A, B. A trip that is on B after 2 jumps, A, C, B, must leave B on jump 3. So there are 3 ways. The transferable idea: draw the whole tree and keep only the branches that finish where the question asks.
solutions.elegant: Work backwards: just before the last jump the frog must be on A or C. After 2 jumps it is on A in 2 ways (A, B, A and A, C, A) and on C in 1 way (A, B, C). Each can then jump to B, so 2 + 1 = 3.

whyOnTest: A tree of 8 trips is small enough to draw but too big to hold in your head, exactly when a tree diagram earns its place.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
